paras: The lynching of Charles Duncan took place in McDowell County, West Virginia, in early March 1888, when a mob took Duncan from officers who were carrying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Duncan had been accused of shooting Milt Hawks, the man he lived with, during a quarrel between Hawks and his wife. A Parkersburg dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Evening Star of Washington predicted that nothing would be done about it.

According to the Parkersburg wire, Mr. and Mrs. Hawks quarreled at Harrisonville, in McDowell County, and Duncan, "a young man boarding with them," took Mrs. Hawks's part. Hawks then began "abusing Duncan, saying he interfered too often in favor of his wife," and the dispute ended with Duncan shooting him through the heart. The Evening Star's version said Hawks attacked Duncan first and that Duncan drew a revolver and killed him instantly. No report states the race of either man.

Duncan fled and hid for two days before a mob found him, in the Star's telling "in a bed" some miles from the scene. One version of the dispatch described this as "a mob formed for the purpose of lynching him if he could not prove his innocence." Duncan was brought before a justice for a preliminary examination, and on the testimony of Mrs. Hawks and of Duncan himself the justice sent him to jail.

The mob had waited for the result, and as Duncan was being taken to jail it overpowered the officers and took him away. The dispatch said that "no resistance to their action was made" and that the men took Duncan to the woods and hanged him to a tree.

No inquest, arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and none of the men was named. The Evening Star wrote that "there will probably be nothing done in the matter, as all the parties bore bad reputations."

The first located report is the Evening Star's of March 5, under the headlines "Hanged on the Way to Jail" and "Lynchers in West Virginia Summarily Dispose of a Murderer." Its account called Duncan's examination proof of guilt through "his own prevarications" and treated the mob as "an indignant populace." The Parkersburg dispatch, dated March 5 and in a slightly revised form March 6, ran in Dakota and Nebraska papers as "The Work of a Mob" and "A Deliberate Mob," reporting the mob's patience without comment.

Digest columns shortened the story to a single line. A "South and West" brief printed in Rhode Island, North Carolina and South Carolina papers said Duncan "killed his employer" at Parkersburg and that "the indignant neighbors lynched him." Closer to the scene, the Virginia Free Press of Charlestown reported that "lynchers hung Chas. Duncan," while the South Branch Intelligencer of Romney, on March 9, reported only that Duncan had shot "Mitch" Hawks on a Friday and had been arrested.

The digest brief placed the killing at Parkersburg, the dateline of the dispatch, while the fuller reports put it at Harrisonville in McDowell County. The March 6 dispatch dated the quarrel to a Sunday, whereas the Romney paper gave Friday.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Duncan
bases: A mob took Duncan, accused of killing Hawks, from officers taking him to jail and hanged him to a tree (A1, A3, A7).

A 'mob' (A3, A7), 'an indignant populace' (A1) or 'indignant neighbors' (A6) seized Duncan from officers after a justice had committed him to jail and hanged him, without legal authority, for the killing of Hawks (A1, A3, A7, A8).

The Parkersburg wire (A3, A7) and the separately worded Evening Star account (A1) agree on the shooting, the examination before a justice and the hanging by a mob, and digest briefs repeat it (A6, A8); the one West Virginia local item found (A5) reports only the shooting and Duncan's arrest.

accounts.label: Parkersburg wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Hawks abused Duncan for siding with his wife and 'the altercation resulted' in Duncan shooting him; after a preliminary trial the mob, which had waited for the result, overpowered the officers and hanged Duncan in the woods without resistance.

accounts.label: Evening Star account
accounts.gist: Hawks attacked Duncan, who drew a revolver; Duncan hid two days 'in a bed', his 'own prevarications proved his guilt' at the examination, and a mob took him from officers and hanged him; nothing was expected to be done because 'all the parties bore bad reputations.'

accounts.label: West Virginia weekly
accounts.gist: Duncan interfered in the Hawkses' quarrel on Friday and shot Hawks dead, and was arrested; no lynching mentioned.

accounts.label: Digest brief
accounts.gist: Duncan killed 'his employer' Hawks at Parkersburg and 'the indignant neighbors lynched him.'

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined that lynchers 'summarily dispose of a murderer', said Duncan's 'prevarications proved his guilt', and expected no action because all parties 'bore bad reputations'.
Western papers ran the Parkersburg dispatch under 'The Work of a Mob' or 'A Deliberate Mob', describing the mob's waiting for the justice's ruling without comment.
Digest columns reduced it to one line, one calling the lynchers 'indignant neighbors' and another simply 'lynchers'.

conflicts.note: Parkersburg is the dispatch dateline; the fuller reports and both West Virginia papers place the events in McDowell county (A1, A5, A8), which is better evidence.

versions.value: Duncan boarded or lived with the Hawkses

conflicts.note: Only the digest brief calls Hawks an employer.
A Sunday shooting (March 4) is hard to reconcile with two days of hiding (A1, A3) before a March 5 dispatch; the earlier March 5 wire text gives no day.
